```{python}
#| include: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": "#F1F5F9",
    "axes.facecolor": "#F1F5F9",
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.edgecolor": "#CBD5E1",
    "axes.labelsize": 12,
    "axes.labelcolor": "#334155",
    "xtick.labelsize": 10,
    "ytick.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.color": "#64748B",
    "ytick.color": "#64748B",
    "lines.linewidth": 2.2,
    "font.family": "DejaVu Sans",
    "grid.color": "#E2E8F0",
    "grid.linewidth": 0.7,
    "legend.fontsize": 10,
    "legend.framealpha": 0.92,
    "legend.edgecolor": "#E2E8F0",
    "figure.dpi": 130,
})

TEAL = "#0D9488"
ORANGE = "#F97316"
GREEN = "#22C55E"
NAVY = "#1A3A5C"
RED = "#EF4444"
GRAY = "#94A3B8"
AMBER = "#FBBF24"

np.random.seed(42)
dates = pd.date_range(start="2018-01-01", end="2022-12-31", freq="B")
returns = []

for d in dates:
    if d < pd.Timestamp("2020-03-01"):
        returns.append(np.random.normal(0.0004, 0.008))
    elif d <= pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"):
        returns.append(np.random.normal(-0.0008, 0.035))
    else:
        returns.append(np.random.normal(0.0005, 0.014))

df = pd.DataFrame({"Date": dates, "Return": returns})
df["Price_Index"] = 100 * (1 + df["Return"]).cumprod()
df["MA30"] = df["Price_Index"].rolling(30).mean()
df["Rolling_Volatility"] = df["Return"].rolling(30).std()
df["Period"] = np.where(
    df["Date"] < "2020-03-01",
    "Pre-COVID",
    np.where(df["Date"] <= "2020-06-30", "COVID Shock", "Post-Shock")
)

COVID = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-01")
P_COLORS = {"Pre-COVID": TEAL, "COVID Shock": ORANGE, "Post-Shock": GREEN}

# Simple decomposition example for teaching time series concepts
n = 240
t = np.arange(n)
trend = 50 + 0.06 * t
seasonality = 2.8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 30)
noise = np.random.normal(0, 0.9, n)
series = trend + seasonality + noise
components = pd.DataFrame({
    "Time": t,
    "Trend": trend,
    "Seasonality": seasonality,
    "Noise": noise,
    "Observed_Series": series
})

mean_r = df["Return"].mean()
std_r = df["Return"].std()
df["Anomaly"] = abs(df["Return"] - mean_r) > 3 * std_r
anomalies = df[df["Anomaly"]]
```

## Why This Topic Matters {background-color="#0D1B2A"}

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
Financial data is naturally ordered through time.

A time series approach helps us answer questions like:

- Is there a long-term trend?
- Is the series becoming more unstable?
- Did a sudden shock change the pattern?
- Are recent observations unusual?
:::

::: {}
<div class="dcard" style="border-color:#F97316;">
<h3 style="color:#FBBF24 !important;">Case Example: COVID-19</h3>
<p>COVID-19 is used here only as the example event.</p>
<p>The main focus is <strong style="color:white;">time series analysis</strong>: trend, smoothing, rolling statistics, structural breaks, and anomalies.</p>
</div>
:::
:::

::: {.info}
Simple idea: Time series analysis helps us understand how a pattern changes before, during, and after an important event.
:::

::: {.four-col}
<div class="card card-teal"><h3>1. Time Series Basics</h3><p>What makes time-ordered data different from regular data?</p></div>
<div class="card card-navy"><h3>2. Trend & Smoothing</h3><p>How do we see the bigger pattern behind daily noise?</p></div>
<div class="card card-orange"><h3>3. Rolling Statistics</h3><p>How do we measure changing risk over time?</p></div>

---

## What Is Time Series Analysis?

A **time series** is data collected in time order.

Examples:

| Area | Example |
|---|---|
| Market analytics | Stock returns |
| Marketing | Website traffic |
| Retail | Daily sales |
| Economics | Inflation |
| Operations | Weekly demand |

::: {.info}
The important part is the timestamp. In time series analysis, the order of observations matters.
:::

---

## Anatomy of a Time Series

Most time series can be understood using four simple pieces:

::: {.four-col}
<div class="card card-teal"><h3>Trend</h3><p>The long-term direction of the series.</p></div>
<div class="card card-orange"><h3>Seasonality</h3><p>A repeating pattern, such as weekly or monthly cycles.</p></div>
<div class="card card-green"><h3>Cycles</h3><p>Longer ups and downs caused by business or economic conditions.</p></div>
<div class="card card-navy"><h3>Noise</h3><p>Random movement that is hard to explain.</p></div>
:::

::: {.info}
A good analyst tries to separate signal from noise.
:::

---

## Example: Trend + Seasonality + Noise

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.2))
ax.plot(components["Time"], components["Observed_Series"], color=TEAL, label="Observed Series")
ax.plot(components["Time"], components["Trend"], color=ORANGE, linewidth=2.8, label="Trend")
ax.set_title("A Simple Time Series: Trend + Seasonality + Noise", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.set_xlabel("Time")
ax.set_ylabel("Value")
ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.info}
This chart is not stock data. It is a teaching example showing how a time series can contain both a smooth trend and short-term fluctuations.
:::

## Market Index Over Time

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.25))
ax.axvspan(COVID, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.09, label="COVID Window")
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Price_Index"], color=TEAL, linewidth=2.4, label="Market Index")
ax.axvline(COVID, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--", label="Shock begins")
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Index Value, Base = 100")
ax.set_title("Illustrative Market Index, 2018 to 2022", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.info}
This example is simulated using Python. It is designed to make the time series concepts easy to see without needing external data files.
:::

## Moving Average: Smoothing the Noise

A **moving average** smooths short-term ups and downs.

It helps us see the bigger direction of the series.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.25))
ax.axvspan(COVID, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.09)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Price_Index"], color=GRAY, linewidth=1.2, alpha=0.8, label="Daily Index")
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["MA30"], color=TEAL, linewidth=3.0, label="30-Day Moving Average")
ax.axvline(COVID, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Index Value")
ax.set_title("Moving Average Smooths Short-Term Noise", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.darkbar}
Easy explanation: the gray line is noisy daily movement. The teal line is the smoother underlying pattern.
:::

---

## Prices vs Returns

For time series analysis, prices and returns answer different questions.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
### Price Series
<div class="card card-navy">
<ul>
<li>Shows the level of the market</li>
<li>Often has a trend</li>
<li>Good for visual storytelling</li>
<li>Less useful for measuring daily risk</li>
</ul>
</div>
:::

::: {}
### Return Series
<div class="card card-teal">
<ul>
<li>Shows period-to-period change</li>
<li>Easier to compare across time</li>
<li>Useful for volatility and anomaly detection</li>
<li>Common in time series modeling</li>
</ul>
</div>
:::
:::

<div class="formula">
Return<sub>t</sub> = (Price<sub>t</sub> - Price<sub>t-1</sub>) / Price<sub>t-1</sub>
</div>

---

## Daily Returns Show the Shock More Clearly

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.1))
for period, grp in df.groupby("Period"):
    ax.plot(grp["Date"], grp["Return"], color=P_COLORS[period], linewidth=0.95, alpha=0.88, label=period)
ax.axvline(COVID, color=ORANGE, linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--", alpha=0.9)
ax.axhline(0, color="#CBD5E1", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Daily Return")
ax.set_title("Daily Returns Across Three Time Periods", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.info}
The COVID period shows larger swings. This is the first sign that the time series has changed behavior.
:::

---

## Rolling Statistics

A rolling statistic recalculates a measure over a moving window.

For example, a 30-day rolling average or 30-day rolling volatility.

::: {.three-col}
<div class="card card-teal"><h3>Rolling Mean</h3><p>Tracks the local average over time.</p></div>
<div class="card card-orange"><h3>Rolling Volatility</h3><p>Tracks how unstable the series is over time.</p></div>
<div class="card card-green"><h3>Rolling Window</h3><p>Uses the most recent observations, then moves forward one day.</p></div>
:::

::: {.darkbar}
This is one of the most useful time series ideas because it shows that patterns are not constant.
:::

---

## Rolling Volatility

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.1))
ax.axvspan(COVID, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10, label="COVID Window")
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Rolling_Volatility"], color=RED, linewidth=2.4, label="30-Day Rolling Volatility")
ax.fill_between(df["Date"], df["Rolling_Volatility"], alpha=0.13, color=RED)
ax.axvline(COVID, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Rolling Std Dev of Returns")
ax.set_title("30-Day Rolling Volatility", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
This is the key slide: volatility jumps sharply during COVID, meaning the series entered a more unstable period.
:::

## Comparing Time Periods

```{python}
period_order = ["Pre-COVID", "COVID Shock", "Post-Shock"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.9))

avgs = [df[df["Period"] == p]["Return"].mean() * 100 for p in period_order]
vols = [df[df["Period"] == p]["Return"].std() * 100 for p in period_order]

bars1 = axes[0].bar(period_order, avgs, color=[TEAL, ORANGE, GREEN], edgecolor="white", width=0.55)
axes[0].axhline(0, color="#CBD5E1", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Average Daily Return (%)", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
axes[0].grid(axis="y")

bars2 = axes[1].bar(period_order, vols, color=[TEAL, ORANGE, GREEN], edgecolor="white", width=0.55)
axes[1].set_title("Volatility, Std Dev (%)", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
axes[1].grid(axis="y")

for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=9)

for bar, v in zip(bars1, avgs):
    axes[0].text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, v + 0.004, f"{v:+.3f}%", ha="center", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")

for bar, v in zip(bars2, vols):
    axes[1].text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, v + 0.04, f"{v:.2f}%", ha="center", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")

fig.tight_layout(pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

::: {.info}
The bigger difference is not the average return. The bigger difference is the increase in volatility.
:::

---

## Structural Breaks

A **structural break** happens when the behavior of a time series changes suddenly.

In simple words:

::: {.three-col}
<div class="card card-teal"><h3>Before</h3><p>The series follows one pattern.</p></div>
<div class="card card-orange"><h3>Shock</h3><p>A major event changes behavior.</p></div>
<div class="card card-green"><h3>After</h3><p>The series may follow a new pattern.</p></div>
:::

::: {.darkbar}
COVID can be viewed as a structural break because the volatility pattern changed suddenly around March 2020.
:::

---

## Distribution of Returns

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.9))

for period in period_order:
    axes[0].hist(df[df["Period"] == period]["Return"], bins=45, alpha=0.55, color=P_COLORS[period], label=period, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)
axes[0].set_title("Return Distribution by Period", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Daily Return")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Frequency")
axes[0].axvline(0, color="#CBD5E1", linewidth=1)
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid(axis="y")

data = [df[df["Period"] == p]["Return"].values for p in period_order]
bp = axes[1].boxplot(data, patch_artist=True, medianprops=dict(color=NAVY, linewidth=2), flierprops=dict(marker=".", markersize=3, alpha=0.4))
for patch, col in zip(bp["boxes"], [TEAL, ORANGE, GREEN]):
    patch.set_facecolor(col)
    patch.set_alpha(0.6)
axes[1].set_xticklabels(["Pre-COVID", "COVID\nShock", "Post-Shock"], fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_title("Box Plot: Spread of Returns", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Daily Return")
axes[1].grid(axis="y")

fig.tight_layout(pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

::: {.info}
The COVID distribution is wider, meaning extreme outcomes became more common.
:::

---

## Anomaly Detection

An anomaly is a data point that looks unusual compared with the normal pattern.

Simple rule used here:

<div class="formula">
Anomaly if |Return - Mean Return| > 3 × Standard Deviation
</div>

::: {.info}
This is called the 3-sigma rule. It is simple, easy to explain, and useful for flagging unusually large movements.
:::

---

## Anomaly Map

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.1))
ax.axvspan(COVID, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.09, label="COVID Window")
ax.plot(df[~df["Anomaly"]]["Date"], df[~df["Anomaly"]]["Return"], color=TEAL, linewidth=0.85, alpha=0.65, label="Normal Return")
ax.scatter(anomalies["Date"], anomalies["Return"], color=RED, s=55, zorder=5, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.6, label=f"Anomaly, n = {len(anomalies)}")
ax.axvline(COVID, color=ORANGE, linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--")
ax.axhline(mean_r + 3 * std_r, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.0, linestyle=":", alpha=0.7, label="3-sigma boundary")
ax.axhline(mean_r - 3 * std_r, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.0, linestyle=":", alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(0, color="#CBD5E1", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Daily Return")
ax.set_title("Simple Anomaly Detection in Market Returns", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
Most anomalies cluster around the shock period. This makes anomaly detection a useful early-warning tool.
:::

---

## Time Series Concepts Used

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<div class="step"><div class="step-n">1</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Trend</h4><p>Long-term direction in the series.</p></div></div>
<div class="step"><div class="step-n">2</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Moving Average</h4><p>Smooths short-term noise.</p></div></div>
<div class="step"><div class="step-n">3</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Rolling Volatility</h4><p>Shows changing instability over time.</p></div></div>
:::

::: {}
<div class="step"><div class="step-n">4</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Structural Break</h4><p>Detects a sudden change in behavior.</p></div></div>
<div class="step"><div class="step-n">5</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Distribution Shift</h4><p>Compares how spread changes across periods.</p></div></div>
<div class="step"><div class="step-n">6</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Anomaly Detection</h4><p>Flags unusually extreme observations.</p></div></div>
:::
:::

## Why This Matters

Time series analysis helps decision-makers understand changing behavior.

In this example, it helps answer:

- Did the pattern change during COVID?
- Did the series become more volatile?
- Were there unusual observations?
- Did the shock create a new regime?

::: {.info}
Main point: the value of time series analysis is not just making charts. It is understanding how behavior changes over time.
:::

---

## Key Takeaways

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<div class="card card-teal"><h3>1. Time Order Matters</h3><p>A time series must be analyzed in sequence because yesterday influences today.</p></div>
<div class="card card-navy"><h3>2. Smoothing Helps</h3><p>Moving averages reveal the underlying pattern behind daily noise.</p></div>
:::

::: {}
<div class="card card-orange"><h3>3. Volatility Changes</h3><p>Rolling volatility shows when a series becomes more unstable.</p></div>
<div class="card card-green"><h3>4. Shocks Are Detectable</h3><p>Structural breaks and anomalies help identify unusual periods.</p></div>
:::
:::

## Final Conclusion {background-color="#0D1B2A"}

COVID-19 is a useful example because it shows how quickly a time series can change.

The main lesson is simple:

::: {.dcard style="border-color:#F97316;"}
A time series is not just a line chart. It is a way to study trend, noise, instability, shocks, and unusual behavior over time.
:::

By using Python, we created a simple workflow:

1. Generate a time series example
2. Smooth the trend with moving averages
3. Measure changing volatility
4. Identify structural breaks
5. Flag anomalies
